$comment: Single source of truth for the server-side auth implementations. Both packages/caselaw-auth (TypeScript) and packages/python (Python) implement this, and both load conformance/cases.json at test time by relative path. Never inline those cases into a language's own tests: the anti-drift guarantee depends on there being one copy.
name: caselaw-auth server contract

session_cookie.$comment: A session is signed, not encrypted. The contents are the user's own identity, which they already know; what matters is that they cannot change it. An unsigned cookie would let anyone promote themselves by editing a role.

payload.of: the session object, serialised as JSON

json_serialisation.$comment: Pinned so that a value sealed by either implementation is byte-identical, not merely mutually readable. Divergence here is invisible until someone diffs two cookies.
json_serialisation.non_ascii: emitted as UTF-8, never escaped to \uXXXX
json_serialisation.key_order: insertion order, as constructed by session_from_claims

signature.key: the configured session secret, as UTF-8 bytes
signature.over: the base64url payload string, as UTF-8 bytes

session_cookie.comparison: constant-time; a length mismatch is a mismatch
session_cookie.byte_limit_behaviour: sealing MUST raise when `<name>=<value>` exceeds the limit, rather than return a value the browser will silently discard

session_record.$comment: What sessionFromClaims / session_from_claims builds. Extra keys are permitted and preserved; these are the ones both implementations guarantee.
session_record.roles: realm_access.roles plus resource_access[clientId].roles, de-duplicated, realm roles first
session_record.expiresAt: unix seconds; now + session_ttl_seconds. NOT the token's exp
session_record.idToken: present only when supplied by the caller; kept for id_token_hint at sign-out

unseal.$comment: Returns the session, or nothing. It never raises for untrusted input: a tampered cookie and an absent one lead to the same place, and distinguishing them only tells an attacker which half they got right.
returns_empty_for: payload that is not valid base64url or not valid JSON

audience.$comment: Keycloak does not put the client id in `aud` for a public client's access token; it puts `account` and names the requesting client in `azp`. Verifying `aud` by default therefore rejects every valid token, which reads as the tokens being broken. Callers who want the check pass `azp`.

jwks.retry: exactly one retry against a freshly fetched key set
jwks.retry_excludes: a token that is itself invalid — malformed, expired, wrong issuer, bad signature — is never retried, because it says the same thing twice

errors.invalid_token: raised for anything wrong with the token; distinguishable from a transport failure
errors.backend_unavailable: raised when the key set cannot be fetched, after the retry

cookie_attributes.$comment: Not `strict`: that drops the cookie on the top-level redirect back from the identity provider, leaving the user signed in everywhere except the page they just landed on.
cookie_attributes.secure: true by default; callers set false only for plaintext localhost

naming.$comment: The two implementations are idiomatic in their own language rather than identical in spelling. This maps them.
naming.$comment_keys: Session keys stay camelCase in BOTH languages. They are wire format, not API surface — a cookie sealed by one implementation must unseal in the other, and renaming keys per language would break exactly that.
